pages.text: Once upon a time, there was a little fox named Mimi.
Mimi loved exploring the forest every day.
One day, she found a river sparkling in the sun.
She saw a tiny fish and grew very curious.
Mimi learned that the world has many surprises.
She went home happy, full of new stories.
Bruno the bear cub lost his ball in the park.
Tito the rabbit saw Bruno sad and came to help.
Together they looked behind trees and flowers.
At last they found the ball under a bench.
Bruno smiled and thanked his friend Tito.
They learned that helping friends feels wonderful.

title: The Vowel Who Lost Her Voice

pages.text: The letter A loved singing louder than all the other letters.
One morning, A opened her mouth and no sound came out at all.
Sad and worried, A went to ask her friends E, I, O and U for help.
E said, "Drink some water and rest your throat, little friend."
I brought warm honey, and O told a silly joke to make A smile.
U hummed softly beside her until she fell fast asleep.
The next morning, A woke up and shouted "Aaaaa!" with all her might.
From that day on, A always sings with her vowel friends close by.
The Syllable Train left the Letter Station every single day.
The first carriage carried MA, ME, MI, MO and MU on a trip.
At the next stop, PA, PE, PI, PO and PU jumped aboard, excited.
The train crossed a bridge and the syllables joined together: MA-PA!
That is how the word "mapa" (map) was born, and everyone clapped.
The train kept going, building new words at every single stop.
Mimi was a little mouse who only found things starting with M.
In the morning, she munched melon and mixed berries with honey.
Then she went to the meadow to pick marigolds with her friend Mia.
At night, she slept under the moon, wrapped in a soft, warm blanket.
Mimi always said, "M for me, M for magic, M for my world!"
She fell asleep happy, dreaming of more words starting with M.
Little Felix the cat tried to meow, but only "woof" came out, like a dog.
The other cats giggled quietly, and Felix felt very embarrassed.
A dog named Rex heard him and said, "That's okay, everyone has their own voice."
Felix practiced every day, all alone beside the river.
One morning, he opened his mouth and out came a clear, lovely "meow."
All the cats came to celebrate, and Felix learned that practice pays off.
Red invited all the colors to a big party in the sky.
Yellow brought the sun and lit up the whole room.
Blue brought the sea, and Green brought the leaves from the trees.
When Blue and Yellow danced together, they made bright Green.
Red and Blue mixed together, and elegant Purple appeared.
At the end of the party, a huge rainbow appeared in the sky, all colors together.
Mother duck had five ducklings, and they all went for a walk by the lake.
One duckling stopped to look at a yellow flower and fell behind.
Another duckling followed a butterfly and got lost among the reeds.
Mother duck counted her babies: only three! She grew worried.
She called "quack-quack" loudly, and the two ducklings heard and ran back.
They all gathered together again, and mother said, "Always stay close to me."
The five ducklings swam happily behind their mother, all the way home.
A little seed was planted in the dark, moist soil.
"I want to grow right now!" she said, stomping her tiny roots.
The rain fell gently and said, "Be patient, I will help you grow."
The sun shone every day and warmed the soil all around her.
Day after day, the seed felt bigger, but still saw nothing.
Finally, a tiny green sprout pushed through the earth and saw the light.
The seed had become a plant, and learned that growing takes time.
One night, the children looked up at the sky and the moon wasn't there.
Everyone was scared: without the moon, the sky looked very dark.
A wise owl said, "The moon hasn't disappeared, she's just changing shape."
The next night, a thin sliver of moon appeared, like a smile in the sky.
Each night, the moon grew a little bigger, until she was round again.
The children learned the moon always makes this journey, month after month.
Now, every night, they look up to see the moon's new shape.
Baltasar woke up very early, nervous: it was his first day of school.
He put on his new sweater and his backpack, his heart beating fast.
At the school door, he held his mom's hand tightly and didn't want to go in.
A girl named Sofia smiled and said, "Want to play with me?"
Together, they built a tower of blocks and drew a blue dragon.
When his mom came back, Baltasar didn't even want to leave — he'd made so many friends.
That night, he told his family everything, excited for the next day.

title: The Monster Who Was Afraid of the Dark

pages.text: Grunf was a furry monster who lived under a bed.
Everyone thought monsters weren't afraid of anything, but Grunf was afraid of the dark.
When the light went out, Grunf trembled and hid under a blanket.
One night, a girl named Ana heard him shaking and asked, "Are you okay?"
Grunf confessed his secret, and Ana brought him a small night light.
With the little light on, Grunf saw that the dark was just... dark, nothing more.
Since then, Grunf and Ana are friends and sleep peacefully with the soft light on.
Leonor was visiting her grandparents when she found a stone gate hidden among the brambles.
On the other side stood an old castle, its towers covered in green moss.
A very old guard in rusty armor limped out to greet her.
"This castle was built seven hundred years ago, when King Afonso Henriques fought to make Portugal a kingdom," he said.
Leonor asked why it was so forgotten, and the guard sighed: "No one comes to hear the old stories anymore."
She explored the great hall, where a huge map showed how Portugal grew over the centuries.
In the courtyard, she saw a replica of the caravel ships Portuguese explorers once sailed around the world.
As she left, Leonor promised to return with her school friends, so the castle's stories would never be forgotten again.

title: Tomás Travels Through the Human Body

pages.text: Tomás drank his scientist grandfather's magic potion and shrank to the size of a grain of rice!
He slid down his throat and landed in a pink pool: the stomach, full of juices dissolving food.
Then he traveled through a long tube, the intestines, where nutrients passed into the blood.
A red river appeared: blood, traveling through blood vessels all over the body.
Tomás reached a room that went "thump-thump": the heart, pumping blood nonstop.
He climbed up to two pink balloons that filled and emptied: the lungs, trading fresh air for used air.
Finally, he saw thousands of electric wires in the brain, sending orders to the whole body.
When the potion wore off, Tomás returned to normal size and told his grandfather everything, amazed.
Little Drop lived in the sea, swimming among colorful fish, happy and salty.
One day, the sun warmed her so much she turned into vapor and rose into the sky.
Up there, she met thousands of other droplets, and together they formed a big white cloud.
When the cloud got too heavy, Little Drop fell as rain over a green mountain.
She slid down a stream, joined a river, and passed through a city full of bridges.
A family collected some river water, cleaned it, and Little Drop came out of a kitchen tap.
A girl drank Little Drop from a cup, and later she returned to the sea through the rivers, ready to start again.

title: A Night at the Dinosaur Museum

pages.text: Inês hid in the museum after closing time, to see the dinosaurs just a little longer.
When the lights went out, the Tyrannosaurus Rex bones began to glow softly.
A voice whispered, "Don't be scared, I'm just the museum's night guardian, Professor Bruno."
He explained dinosaurs lived over 65 million years ago, long before humans existed.
He showed the Triceratops, with three horns for protection, and the Pteranodon, which flew but wasn't a true dinosaur.
A huge fossil footprint showed how a Brachiosaurus was as tall as a five-story building.
Professor Bruno explained a giant meteorite hit Earth and changed the climate forever, ending the dinosaurs' time.
In the morning, Inês was found asleep beside the skeleton, dreaming of giant creatures.

title: The Mystery of the Missing Magnet

pages.text: During science class, the horseshoe-shaped magnet vanished from the teacher's desk.
Diana, the most curious kid in class, decided to investigate like a real detective.
First, she remembered magnets attract iron, steel, and nickel, but not wood or plastic.
She scanned the room and saw paper clips oddly sticking to her classmate Rui's backpack.
She carefully opened the backpack, and there was the magnet, hidden under a book.
Rui confessed he'd taken it to try at home, but forgot to bring it back.
The teacher explained magnets have two poles, North and South, and like poles repel while opposite poles attract.
In the end, everyone did an experiment together, watching the magnet pull small nails, and Diana felt like a real scientist.
The one-euro coin was born in a factory and kept in a bank, shiny and new.
One day, it was given to Mr. Manuel as change for buying bread at the bakery.
Mr. Manuel kept it in his pocket and later gave it to his granddaughter Carlota as allowance.
Carlota wanted to buy ice cream, but decided to save half the money in her piggy bank.
The other coin went for ice cream, and the traveling euro stayed in the ice cream seller's pocket.
The seller used it to pay the shop's electricity bill, and it traveled on to an energy company.
The coin learned that money passes from hand to hand, helping people trade things they need.
Meanwhile, in Carlota's piggy bank, the other half of the money slowly grew towards a bigger dream: a new bicycle.

title: The Red Backpack's Trip Around the World

pages.text: Marta's red backpack was magic: every time she slept, it took her to a different country.
On the first night, she woke up in France, near the Eiffel Tower, and learned to say "bonjour" to everyone.
She ate warm croissants and watched painters working by the Seine river.
On the second night, she arrived in Japan, where she saw pink mountains covered in cherry blossoms.
She learned to bow to say hello and tried eating with chopsticks for the first time.
On the third night, she went to Egypt, where she saw giant pyramids and heard stories of ancient pharaohs.
A guide told her the pyramids are over four thousand years old, built with huge stone blocks.
On the last night, she arrived in Brazil, danced samba at a colorful party, and tasted sweet fruit under the hot sun.
When Marta woke up in her own bed, she smiled: the backpack had shown her the world is huge and full of wonderful things.
At the Science Club, three friends — Rita, Zé and Nuno — solved mysteries using only observation and experiments.
One day, the plants in the school garden began wilting with no explanation, and the teacher asked the trio for help.
Rita suggested forming a hypothesis: maybe they lacked water, or maybe there was too much sun.
Zé measured how much water each plant received, while Nuno noted the hours of sunlight on each bed.
They discovered the wiltiest plants were near a pipe with a small hole, letting all the water leak out.
They fixed the pipe with the gardener's help, and two weeks later the plants bloomed again.
The trio learned science begins with a good question, follows with careful tests, and ends with conclusions based on evidence.
Since then, the Science Club became known at school as "the detectives who solve any mystery with the scientific method."
In grandma's attic, Duarte found an old pocket watch that, when opened, created a swirl of light.
Without meaning to, he touched the hands and was transported to 1140, when King Afonso Henriques fought to separate Portugal from the Kingdom of León.
He saw soldiers building stone castles and heard stories about the Battle of São Mamede, decisive for independence.
The watch spun again and Duarte appeared in 1497, at the Lisbon docks, beside Vasco da Gama, about to sail toward India.
He learned about navigation instruments, like the astrolabe, which helped sailors find their way by the stars.
Next, he traveled to 1755, the day of the great Lisbon earthquake, and saw how the city was rebuilt by the Marquis of Pombal.
Finally, he arrived in 1974, witnessing the Carnation Revolution, when people placed flowers in soldiers' guns to ask for peace and freedom.
When he returned to the attic, Duarte realized Portugal's history was made of courage, discovery, and hope.
The young explorers set off on an expedition to discover Earth's most incredible ecosystems.
First, they crossed the Amazon Rainforest, learning it produces about 20% of the planet's oxygen.
They saw monkeys, toucans, and leafcutter ants, and understood how each species depends on the others to survive.
Then they headed to the Sahara Desert, where daytime temperatures can pass 45 degrees, but nights get very cold.
A Bedouin guide explained how camels store fat in their humps and can travel days without drinking water.
The expedition continued to Antarctica, where the explorers saw huge icebergs and emperor penguins protecting their eggs from the extreme cold.
Finally, they dove into the Great Barrier Reef in Australia and were amazed by the amount of life hidden underwater.
At the end of the trip, everyone agreed: protecting these places means protecting the balance of the whole planet.
Every Friday, a group of kids met in Sara's garage to invent new things.
That week's goal was to create something to help Miguel's grandmother, who struggled reaching high objects.
First, they brainstormed, writing every idea on the board, even the craziest ones.
Then they picked the best idea: an extendable arm made from PVC pipes and a recycled claw.
They built a first prototype, but it broke while trying to reach a cereal box.
Instead of giving up, they analyzed what went wrong and reinforced the joint with extra-strong tape.
On the second try, the extendable arm worked perfectly, and Miguel's grandmother loved the gift.
They learned engineering's most important lesson: failure isn't the end, just a step toward a better idea.
Leandro received a message from a stranger asking for his address and his parents' phone number.
Not knowing what to do, he showed the message to his older sister Carolina, part of a group called "Internet Guardians."
Carolina explained the first rule: never share personal info, like address, school, or phone, with strangers online.
The second rule was that a strong password mixes letters, numbers and symbols, and should never be shared, even with friends.
She also explained that not everything online is true, and you should always confirm information with a trusted adult.
Together, they blocked the stranger and reported the message on the app, exactly as a trusted adult had taught them.
Carolina reminded Leandro: "If something online makes you uncomfortable, always tell a trusted adult, without fear."
From that day on, Leandro also became an Internet Guardian, helping other classmates browse safely.
A rumor started spreading at school: "the cafeteria is closing forever next week!"
The journalism club, led by Beatriz, decided to investigate before believing or spreading the news.
First they asked: "Who said this? Where was it published? Is there a reliable source?"
They found the news came from an authorless message, shared phone to phone, with no proof at all.
They went to talk directly with the school principal, the most reliable source on this matter.
The principal explained the cafeteria would only close for two days for cleaning, not forever.
Beatriz and her team wrote a short article for the school newspaper, explaining the truth with clear facts.
Everyone learned the golden rule: always check the source before sharing news, and never spread something without being sure.
The crew of the ship Hope prepared for the hardest landing of their mission: touching down on Mars.
Commander Alice told the crew the journey had taken seven months, covering about 480 million kilometers.
As the ship entered the Martian atmosphere, it shook hard: Mars's air is much thinner than Earth's, making braking harder.
After a perfect landing, the crew stepped out and saw an orange sky, covered in fine dust that gives Mars its reddish color.
They collected rock samples near an ancient dry riverbed, looking for signs that Mars once had liquid water.
Engineer Tomás tested a small robot that extracted oxygen from carbon dioxide in the Martian air, an important step for future human missions.
At night, they saw Mars's two small moons, Phobos and Deimos, crossing the dark sky much faster than our Moon.
Before leaving, Commander Alice left a plaque: "We were here, on behalf of all humankind, in search of knowledge."

title: The Mystery of the Seven Capitals

pages.text: An old geographer left a riddle hidden in a chest: seven clues leading to seven capital cities of the world.
The first clue read: "Where the Tagus meets the ocean, and streets climb up hills." It was Lisbon, capital of Portugal.
The second: "An iron tower points to the sky, in a city cut by a famous river." It was Paris, France.
The third spoke of "a great wall nearby and a forbidden palace in the heart of the city" — Beijing, China.
The fourth described "seven ancient hills and ruins where gladiators once fought" — Rome, Italy.
The fifth mentioned "old gates and a wall that once split a city in two" — Berlin, Germany.
The sixth spoke of "squares full of dancing and a museum with famous master paintings" — Madrid, Spain.
The last clue led to "a river called the Thames and a giant clock that chimes every hour" — London, England.
At the bottom of the chest, the explorers found a world map and a note: "Each capital holds a story; go meet them with respect."
